title: Language Sample Analysis Practices in a Multilingual and Diglossic Context: A Survey of Speech-Language Pathologists in German-Speaking Switzerland
abstract: Purpose: This study investigated the frequency, purpose, target groups, and methods of language sample analysis (LSA) among speech-language pathologists (SLPs) in German-speaking Switzerland. LSA is particularly relevant in linguistically diverse and underresearched contexts such as diglossic settings, where everyday spoken language differs from standardized varieties. Method: A survey was conducted among 550 SLPs in German-speaking Switzerland. Descriptive statistics were used to analyze the data, focusing on reported use, target demographics, and analytical methods concerning LSA. Results: Compared with previous research from English-speaking countries, LSA is used by a larger proportion of SLPs in Switzerland. Consistent with prior findings, Swiss SLPs primarily employ individualized approaches rather than established protocols. LSA is most frequently conducted in younger children, while the use of assistive tools remains low. Furthermore, SLPs mainly focus on microstructural parameters (e.g., morphology–syntax) rather than on macrostructural parameters during analysis. title: Effects of Naturalistic Developmental Behavioral Intervention Strategies and Visual Scene Displays on Autistic Children's Joint Engagement
abstract: Purpose: Naturalistic developmental behavioral intervention (NDBI) and visual scene displays (VSDs), a type of augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), are research-supported practices focused on naturalistic instruction and increasing social communication skills in young autistic children. The purpose of our study was to extend previous research to understand the effects of embedding VSDs within a dynamic play-based NDBI for young autistic children. Method: We employed a randomized multiple-baseline single-case experimental design across three participants to evaluate the effects of (a) NDBI strategies and (b) NDBI strategies plus aided AAC modeling and just-in-time (JIT) programming of VSDs on joint engagement in young autistic children. Results: When NDBI strategies were introduced, there was a large positive effect on child joint engagement and a corresponding large negative effect on child isolated attention. After aided AAC modeling and JIT programming were introduced, child joint engagement and isolated attention outcomes were mixed. Conclusions: The findings of the current study show promise to using VSDs within dynamic play-based NDBIs as a communication support.

title: Investigating Variability and Malleability of Speech-Language Pathologists' Responsive Talk With Children: An Early-Efficacy Trial
abstract: Purpose: The purposes of this early-stage efficacy study were to examine speech-language pathologists' (SLPs') use of responsive talk with children and to determine the extent to which responsive talk can be modified through brief clinician education or an in situ, tablet-based feedback system, GENIE, that provided real-time prompts to use responsive talk. Method: Eleven SLPs (certified clinicians and graduate students) and 11 typically developing preschool-aged children participated in a quasi-experimental study. SLPs were paired with a randomly assigned child to complete two structured intervention sessions to assess responsive talk. In the first session, SLPs used their business-as-usual practices, whereas in the second session, SLPs were randomly assigned to receive clinician education or the in situ GENIE prompts, representing a planned variation in instructing SLPs to use responsive talk during intervention. title: Communication Difficulties and Management: The Lived Experience of Individuals With Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration Spectrum Disorders
abstract: Purpose: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) is the neuropathology that underlies a collection of progressive clinical syndromes typically classified by the initial/primary symptom. For example, individuals with loss of word meaning as a first manifestation are often diagnosed with the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia. Growing evidence suggests that language and communication can be impacted in all clinical syndromes across the FTLD spectrum, but the functional relevance of these symptoms has yet to be explored. Method: The Frontotemporal Degeneration (FTD) Insights Survey is the largest community survey of individuals affected by FTLD. It was administered online and included questions related to demographics, symptoms, life participation, quality of life, and experiences with and hopes for treatment. title: Core Lexicon Analysis of a Storytelling Task in Korean-Speaking Individuals With Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to validate newly developed, age-stratified Korean core lexicon (CL) checklists and evaluate their clinical utility in assessing discourse production in persons with aphasia (PWA) using a culturally familiar storytelling task. Method: Thirty-six PWA and 36 age- and education-matched cognitively healthy adults (CHAs) participated in a Korean picture-based storytelling task. Percentage of core nouns and verbs were calculated using age-specific checklists and compared across group (CHAs vs. PWA) and lexical category (noun vs. verb). We also examined whether core noun and verb percentages were associated with aphasia severity and which word class significantly predicted severity. Results: PWA exhibited significantly lower percentage of CL than CHAs, with a larger noun–verb difference observed in PWA than in CHAs. Pearson correlation analyses showed that both core nouns and verbs were significantly and positively associated with aphasia severity. title: Pushing the Limits on Learning Gender-Affirming Voice: An Autoethnography From a Client
abstract: Gender-affirming voice work differs fundamentally from other speech-language pathology work. Rather than addressing pathology in communication, gender-affirming voice work teaches clients how to change behavior, which is limited in part by how gender-diverse people interact with their social environment. Integrating my original theory of gender with my personal experience learning gender-affirming voice, I explain possible obstacles gender-diverse people face as well as recommendations to speech-language pathologists to mitigate them. In particular, gender-diverse people may exhibit difficulties in auditory processing, vocal biomechanics, and generalization into gender expression. However, despite unique challenges presented by gender-affirming voice work, my experience is overall positive and worth the effort.

title: The Management of Swallowing Disorders in Children With Spinal Muscular Atrophy Type 1: A Scoping Review
abstract: Purpose: Spinal muscular atrophy Type 1 (SMA1) is a rare autosomal recessive neuromuscular disorder with progressive muscle weakness and atrophy. Dysphagia is common among children with SMA1, and its complications are frequently documented. This scoping review aimed to describe the management of swallowing disorders in this population. Method: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, four electronic databases were searched (PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and Cochrane Library) for studies on children with SMA1. We investigated the management of swallowing disorders in children with SMA1, including methods and protocols used to assess swallowing and feeding, and treatment option. The quality of included studies was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklists; two independent researchers conducted study selection and data extraction. Results: Thirty-eight studies with a total of 1,784 SMA1 patients were included. title: Variety Matters: Measuring Semantic Verb Types in Conversation Following ECoLoGiC Treatment for People With Moderate or Severe Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: Expanding Communication and Language Opportunities Generated in Conversation Treatment (ECoLoGiC-Tx) is a conversation treatment designed to improve the everyday language abilities of people with moderate-to-severe aphasia. Previous research reported improved use of basic syntactic structures during posttreatment conversations. Although ECoLoGic-Tx does not specifically target verb use, it may change the frequency and/or types of verbs used during conversation. Semantic verb type analysis categorizes verbs by their intended meaning. Each of the five semantic verb types serves a unique function during discourse, and difficulty using verbs within and across semantic categories may limit what is shared during everyday interactions. Because verbs play an essential role in conversation, this study explores if ECoLoGiC-Tx changed the frequency and semantic categories of verbs used by people with aphasia (PWA). title: Feasibility and Efficacy of a Hybrid Delivery Model of the Categorization Program for Individuals With Chronic Traumatic Brain Injury: A Pilot Study
abstract: Purpose: The present study examined the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of a hybrid, telehealth-adapted delivery of the Categorization Program (CP), an evidence-based cognitive rehabilitation intervention, for adults with chronic moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury (msTBI) who were living in the community and not engaged in ongoing rehabilitation services. It was hypothesized that the telehealth-adapted CP would demonstrate high feasibility and lead to improvements in intervention-specific and standardized neuropsychological outcomes. Method: This study employed a single-group, pre–post intervention design with follow-up assessments. Adults aged 18–65 years with msTBI sustained at least 1 year prior to enrollment were recruited from hospital and rehabilitation center databases. Participants completed a baseline neuropsychological assessment, followed by the eight-level, hierarchically structured CP intervention delivered primarily via telehealth. Neuropsychological measures were administered pre-intervention and post-intervention, while CP-specific measures were administered pre-intervention and post-intervention and at 4- and 8-week follow-ups. title: Applying the Social Communication Implementable and Applicable Lens Framework to Intervention
abstract: Purpose: The Social Communication Implementable and Applicable Lens (SoCIAL) is a framework that offers a comprehensive, context-sensitive approach to the assessment and intervention of social communication for individuals with brain injury. Building upon foundational models such as the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, the Model of Cognitive-Communication Competence, and the Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System, SoCIAL emphasizes the interplay of identity, skills, demands, and environment in shaping communicative participation and quality of life. This clinical focus article demonstrates the application of the SoCIAL framework to evidence-based intervention to support holistic, person-centered care. Through a detailed clinical case study, we illustrate how intervention targets and ingredients, collaborative goal setting, and contextual flexibility can be addressed in the context of the framework. title: Priorities and Fractures in DeafPlus Augmentative and Alternative Communication Decision-Making Teams
abstract: Purpose: Children who are DeafPlus often engage in multiple services across a range of settings. For children who are DeafPlus using augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), decisions require further distributed expertise when communication planning. However, the processes that these teams engage in when decision making for this cohort remains underexamined. Method: This qualitative study analyzed the transcripts of three focus groups to gain insight into how professionals perceive and experience aspects of multidisciplinary interaction such as negotiating roles, authority, and communication approaches specifically for students who are DeafPlus using AAC. title: The Relationship Between Dynamic Assessment of Analogical Reasoning and Syntax in French-Speaking Children With and Without Developmental Language Disorder
abstract: Purpose: According to usage-based theories of language development, typically developing (TD) children rely on analogical reasoning (AR) to learn syntactic structures. However, children with developmental language disorder (DLD) demonstrate difficulties in AR, which could contribute to explaining their difficulties in acquiring syntactic structures. While previous studies have reported no link between nonverbal AR and syntax using static assessment, we shifted focus onto dynamic assessment to explore the relationship between these two domains' learning potential in a French-speaking population. Method: Ninety-seven TD children (25 bilingual) and 98 children with DLD (40 bilingual; M age = 8;8 [years;months]) were assessed by using (a) a static task of AR; (b) a static task of syntax; (c) a dynamic task of AR, with prompts assisting the learner to analyze the analogy required to complete the matrix; and (d) a dynamic task of syntax targeting six structures, with prompts based on syntactic priming. title: Service Delivery Barriers in Pediatric Feeding Disorder: A Path Forward
abstract: Purpose: This article examines barriers and facilitators to the care of children with pediatric feeding disorder (PFD), a complex condition that impacts individuals, families, medical institutions, and communities. Method: This clinical focus article was developed through a targeted literature synthesis and conceptual analysis leading to the identification and grouping of care barriers. Results: Multiple barriers affecting professionals and caregivers were identified, including limitations in resources, clinical tools, care coordination, accessibility, and caregiver-related factors. Conclusions: The identification of barriers reveals the need for unified strategic approaches to improve care efforts. Five key initiatives are proposed: advancing research, policy, and guidelines; providing PFD-specific professional training; expanding access to care; strengthening support systems; and enhancing caregiver education and engagement.

title: What Temperament Can Tell Us About Language Development of Late-Talking Toddlers
abstract: Purpose: The primary aim of this study was to compare temperamental traits in typically developing and late-talking toddlers. A secondary aim was to evaluate potential associations between language skills and temperament within each group. Method: Caregivers of typically developing ( n = 21) and late-talking ( n = 21) toddlers, aged 18–35 months, completed a brief measure of temperament (Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire–Very Short Form) and expressive vocabulary (MacArthur–Bates Communicative Development Inventories: Words and Sentences). Toddlers' expressive and receptive language skills were also directly assessed using the Mullen Scales of Early Learning. Results: There were no significant group differences on the temperament measurement between general constructs; however, late talkers showed lower levels of sensory discomfort and positive anticipation compared to typical talkers. title: Craniofacial Education in Accredited Graduate Speech-Language Pathology Programs: National Patterns in Coursework and Clinical Training
abstract: Purpose: This study provides an updated national examination of craniofacial education across accredited graduate speech-language pathology programs in the United States. Method: A survey was distributed to 289 accredited graduate speech-language pathology programs. Ninety-nine programs completed all or part of the survey. Publicly available curricular materials were reviewed for nonresponding programs, and brief follow-up correspondence was conducted when necessary. The final data set included 281 programs. Data were analyzed descriptively to characterize coursework structure and clinical training opportunities. Results: Among the 281 programs analyzed, 19.9% offered a dedicated and required craniofacial course and 11.4% offered a dedicated elective course. The majority of programs (68.7%) reported covering craniofacial content exclusively through embedded instruction. Sixty-three percent of programs reported offering clinical experiences involving individuals with craniofacial conditions, although most indicated that fewer than 25% of students engaged in these experiences. title: Screening Beyond First Words: A Scoping Review of Speech and Language Screening Tools and Approaches for 2- and 3-Year-Olds
abstract: Purpose: The task of being able to accurately and efficiently identify children in the early years at risk of future speech sound and/or language disorders remains elusive. To progress toward more accurate identification, the breadth of skills examined in current screening tools and approaches needs to be determined. Our purpose was to (a) understand the key characteristics of screening tools and approaches for children aged 2–3 years, (b) determine the psychometric quality of screening tools and approaches, and (c) identify the early years health and education professionals who screen toddlers' speech and language skills. Method: A scoping review was conducted following Arksey and O'Malley's (2005) methodological framework and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension guidelines. A systematic search of the literature was conducted, and the data were described through data extraction, quality appraisal, percentage and frequency counts, and a narrative synthesis. abstract: Purpose: This preliminary study aimed to (a) determine whether the frequency and intensity of emotional facial expressions during personal narrative discourse are different for people with aphasia (PWA) than for adults without aphasia and (b) explore the relationship between the frequency and intensity of emotional facial expressions and aphasia severity. Method: Fifty-two participants, including 26 PWA and 26 control participants, were randomly selected from Aphasia Bank, a protocoled database with video recordings of both people with and without aphasia. Two video-recorded narrative discourse samples, a stroke/illness story and an important life event story, from each participant were used. title: The Effects of Immersive Virtual Reality on Discourse Production in Younger and Older Adults
abstract: Purpose: Discourse production tasks are widely used to assess language across clinical and research contexts. Virtual reality (VR) offers an alternative discourse elicitation modality by providing immersive 3-D environments that may influence language production differently from traditional picture-based tasks. This study examined whether immersive VR affects discourse production compared with traditional picture description tasks as well as how younger and older adults perceive the usability and acceptability of and relative preference for each modality. Method: Forty-five younger and 33 older neurotypical adults described two widely studied images (Cookie Theft and Cat Rescue), presented either as colored 2-D images or as immersive 3-D VR environments. title: Evaluating Intrarater Reliability of Nasopharyngoscopy Ratings Made by Speech-Language Pathologists in a Clinical Versus Research Setting
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to evaluate intrarater reliability for nasopharyngoscopy ratings of velopharyngeal closure across two contexts: ratings made in a clinical setting and ratings made in a research setting using standardized rating definitions. Method: Five speech-language pathologists participated in this study. Two assessments of intrarater reliability were performed: between ratings from clinical reports and re-ratings made in a research setting and videos re-rated twice in a research setting. Nasopharyngoscopy ratings analyzed included velopharyngeal closure pattern, total percent closure, and extent of velar movement. Reliability was calculated using Cohen's kappa and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). title: Preliminary Evidence for the Effects of Bilingual ECoLoGiC Treatment for People With Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: The focus of this preliminary study is to report the effects of bilingual Expanding Communication and Language Opportunities Generated in Conversation Treatment (ECoLoGiC-Tx) on formal measures of language, functional communication, and patient/family-reported outcomes (P/FROMs) in bilingual people with aphasia (PWA). Method: Two bilingual participants, P1 (70 years old, Hebrew–English, moderate Broca's aphasia) and P2 (73 years old, Yiddish–English, mild anomic aphasia), participated in this quasi-experimental, pretest/posttest case series, with a follow-up session 6 weeks after the bilingual intervention. The use of the ECoLoGiC-Tx model for bilingual PWA incorporated dual-language use, including code-switching, translanguaging, and translation, as natural communicative choices. title: Communication Changes Following SPEAK OUT!: Perspectives of People With Parkinson's Disease and Their Care Partners
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to examine whether the SPEAK OUT!® Therapy Program impacts patient self-reported outcomes in communicative effectiveness and voice function for people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) and hypokinetic dysarthria and to identify patient factors (e.g., cognition, dysarthria severity) that influence treatment response. In addition, we examined how care partners perceived changes in PwPD's communicative effectiveness following SPEAK OUT! and how self-ratings and care partner ratings compared to each other. Method: Twenty-seven PwPD completed the SPEAK OUT! Therapy Program via telehealth. Two patient-reported outcome measures (i.e., Communication Effectiveness Survey [CES] and Voice Handicap Index-10 [VHI-10]) were collected at three pretreatment and three posttreatment timepoints. A subset of 13 PwPD had care partners who also provided CES ratings at pre- and posttreatment timepoints. title: Analysis of Speech-Language Pathologist and Preprofessional Student Observations of Parent–Child Play Interactions
abstract: Purpose: Initial clinical observations help establish a strengths-based caregiver coaching relationship and guide intervention planning. This study examined what caregiver–child communication strategies speech-language pathologists (SLPs) and master's-level graduate students prioritize when making an initial observation of a naturalistic play interaction. Method: Twenty American Speech-Language-Hearing Association–certified SLPs and 20 master's-level graduate students reviewed videos of caregiver–child play interactions and answered open-ended questions related to what they observed in the interactions. Responses were analyzed using directed content analysis focused on strategies related to environmental arrangement and language facilitation relevant to language development. Results: Across 1,469 coded thought units, participants' comments centered on teachable caregiver actions (facilitation strategies) more than environmental features. title: Exploring the Self-Perceived Role of South African Speech-Language Pathologists in Youth Correctional Facilities
abstract: Purpose: Justice-involved youth (JIY) represent a vulnerable population with a well-documented elevated risk for language disorder compared to their nonoffending peers. Research also suggests that JIY with language disorder are more likely to reoffend after release. Despite this, the involvement of speech-language pathologists (SLPs) in JIY rehabilitation in South Africa remains limited. This study explored the perceptions of South African SLPs regarding their potential roles in youth correctional facilities. Method: A cross-sectional, mixed-method online survey design was used. title: Effectiveness of an Online Perceptual Evaluation of Voice Training Platform on the Rater Reliability in Novice Raters
abstract: Purpose: The primary aim of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of an online perceptual evaluation of voice training platform in improving the rater reliability of novice raters. The secondary aim was to determine the relationship between the training duration and rating accuracy. Method: Forty-two speech-language pathology students participated in this study. Training was conducted using an online training platform over a 12-week period. The online training platform was developed based on perceptual learning theory and includes three main components: (a) familiarization with vocal parameters, (b) training with a single vocal parameter, and (c) training with multiple vocal parameters. Students were instructed to use the training platform to practice auditory–perceptual ratings both inside and outside the classroom. All voice samples included three vocal tasks: sustained vowels, passage reading, and conversational speech. title: Engaging Children in Brain–Computer Interface (BCI) Development: Utilizing an Interactive iPad Tool to Capture Picture-Based P300-Based BCI Augmentative and Alternative Communication Design Preferences
abstract: Introduction: P300-based brain–computer interface augmentative and alternative communication (P300-BCI-AAC) systems show promise for supporting communication for children with severe speech and physical impairments. However, little is known about how children prefer these displays to be designed. This study examined children's design choices and the rationales guiding those choices to inform the development of user-centered, pediatric BCI-AAC displays. Method: Thirty-eight typically developing children (8–12 years of age) used a P300-BCI-AAC design application to create their preferred picture-based interface. Participants selected features such as color, animation, and overlays. Semistructured interviews followed to capture reasons for their decisions. title: Social Disadvantage and Language Disorder: Is Dissociating Possible?
abstract: Purpose: We (a) investigated whether children of lower socioeconomic status (SES) are at a greater risk of developmental language disorder (DLD) than children of higher SES, based on standardized assessment; (b) identified the language skills most strongly affected by SES; and (c) examined which standardized and naturalistic measures best differentiate DLD in children from lower SES backgrounds. Method: We compared Russian-speaking children of middle SES (urban) and low SES (rural) on standardized language tasks. title: A Qualitative Evidence Synthesis of Communication Partner Training: Exploring the Experiences of Communication Partners and People With Acquired Brain Injury
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to explore the experiences of adult communication partners (CPs) of individuals with acquired brain injury (ABI) who received communication training and, where reported, the experiences of individuals with ABI who attended or participated in the training. Method: A qualitative evidence synthesis was conducted. Electronic searches were completed in CINAHL Ultimate, APA PsycInfo, APA PsycArticles, Medline, Embase, AMED, Scopus, NeuroBITE, and PubMed for studies published until August 2025. Included studies described an intervention directed at adult CPs where the program focus was on improving communicative participation for adults post-ABI. title: Interprofessional Education Improves Understanding of Aspiration Pneumonia Risk Factors and Interprofessional Competence Among Dental Hygiene and Speech-Language Pathology Students
abstract: Purpose: Poor oral health and oropharyngeal dysphagia are modifiable risk factors for aspiration pneumonia. Dental hygienists (DHs) and speech-language pathologists (SLP) provide specialized services to individuals with these issues and may benefit from interdisciplinary knowledge in these areas. The objective of this study was to assess how an interprofessional education (IPE) event influenced students' knowledge and competence in working with individuals at risk for aspiration pneumonia. Method: The current study was a prospective, within-subjects cohort design. Participants included speech-language pathology and dental hygiene students ( N = 52). The 3-hr IPE event provided didactic and hands-on training that focused on the modifiable risk factors for aspiration pneumonia. Outcomes were assessed with a content assessment, the Interprofessional Education Collaborative (IPEC) Competency Self-Assessment Tool (Version 3), the Interprofessional Attitudes Scale (IPAS), and written feedback. title: Upward Effortful Pitch Glide as a Predictor of Pharyngeal Constriction in Individuals With Upper Versus Lower Motor Neuron Lesions
abstract: Purpose: This study tested the validity of using nasoendoscopy ratings of volitional maximum pharyngeal constriction (PCmax) during nasoendoscopy recordings of effortful upward pitch glide to predict pharyngeal area at maximum constriction (PAM) during swallowing recordings (VFSSs) in individuals with upper motor neuron (UMN) versus lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions. Method: Retrospective analysis of electronic medical records identified individuals with UMN or LMN lesions who underwent both VFSS and nasoendoscopy within 3 months. Blinded expert judges rated the degree and symmetry of PCmax in paired nasoendoscopic images of quiet breathing (minimum pharyngeal constriction) and highest pitch production (PCmax). title: The Impact of Hospitals on Language Learning: A Case Study of a 3-Year-Old Boy With Developmental Delay Who Needed Augmentative and Alternative Communication
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this pilot study was to describe the language learning contexts experienced by a young child with global developmental delays and limited speech during an inpatient stay. Method: An observational case study was completed to describe the language learning contexts during the inpatient stay of a 3-year-old child with global developmental delay. Six health care providers participated and interacted with him during the 16-hr observational period over two consecutive days. Interactions were video-recorded and coded, and researcher memos were used to describe environmental variables. Results: During the observation period, the child interacted with at least one adult partner for a total of 6 hr. During the remaining 10 hr, he did not have human contact. His stay was characterized by extended periods without adult interaction interspersed with concentrated periods of linguistic input by providers during activities related to medical procedures, mealtimes, daily care, and therapy sessions. title: Response to the Letters by Chang and Bernstein Ratner
abstract: Purpose: In our original article, we draw attention to the lifetime quality-of-life impairment that can result from childhood stuttering—hence, the need for immediate intervention after onset. We drew on existing experimental outcomes that parent speech-rate reduction and increased interturn speaker latency may reduce stuttering. We developed a two-factor treatment protocol based on those variables in combination and showed its clinical viability, suggesting that it would be a suitable target for Phase I–IV clinical trials. Chang and Bernstein Ratner wrote letters to the editor on our article, to which we respond. Conclusions: Our response to these letters to the editor covers the following issues raised by Chang and Bernstein Ratner: mechanisms of action for the proposed treatment, the evidence base for the treatment, plans to explore its treatment effects, and the need to verify its safety.

title: Variability of Preschool Stuttering During a Day
abstract: Purpose: Severity ratings (SRs) of children's stuttering assigned by parents and speech-language pathologists (SLPs) have advantages over methods based on stuttering counts. They are valid, simple, and convenient; without cost; and can be used without the child's awareness. The aim of this project was to study, for the first time, the use of an SR scale by parents and SLPs to track stuttering severity for preschool children over a typical day. For that purpose, we used 10 case studies. Method: Participants were 10 preschool children who stuttered (3–4 years of age) and their parents. Each child's speech was audio-recorded by their parent for an entire day at home, commencing at approximately 8:00 a.m. During that day, an SLP made a randomly timed phone call, during which a 10-min sample of the child's speech was audio-recorded. At the end of the day, both before and after training in the use of a 10-point scale, parents assigned a “typical” SR score for their child's speech for the day. title: Narrative Tell and Retell in Mandarin–English Bilingual Children
abstract: Purpose: Speech-language pathologists often adopt narrative tasks to assess bilingual children's language skills. However, limited research guides clinical decisions about elicitation method, assessment language, and interpretation of results for specific bilingual populations. The present study examined the impact of elicitation method (tell vs. retell) and language (Mandarin vs. English) on macro- and microstructure narrative skills in Mandarin–English bilingual children. Method: We collected narrative tell and retell samples from 79 Mandarin–English bilingual children using the Multilingual Assessment Instrument for Narratives both online and in-person and analyzed macro- and microstructure measures in each language. Results: For macrostructure, children produced better narrative retells than tells across story structure, story complexity, and number of internal state terms, with cross-linguistic differences only in story structure (Mandarin > English). Code-switching did not significantly impact macrostructure scores. title: Developing a Clinically Practical Tool to Evaluate Directed Caregiver Communication in Early Intervention: A Pilot Study of the Tool's Reliability and Validity
abstract: Purpose: Early intervention (EI) relies heavily on directed caregiver communication (DCC), yet most clinical tools focus primarily on the child. This pilot study examined the reliability and validity of the Directed Caregiver Communication Assessment Tool (DCC-AT), which was developed by the authors to describe caregiver communication during naturalistic caregiver–child interactions. Method: This study used secondary data from the Early Communication Indicator for Autism (ECI-A), a naturalistic, 6-min play-based assessment during caregiver–child interaction. Participants included 10 autistic and 10 non-autistic children, all 36 months of age or younger, with test–retest videos for the autistic group resulting in 30 ECI-A videos. Coders used the DCC-AT to assess the types and frequencies of DCC strategies across four primary categories using partial interval coding. Result: Analyses showed that the DCC-AT captured observed variation in DCC and demonstrated strong interrater reliability. title: Comparing Traditional Motor Speech Practice to Contextualized Speech Practice in Preschoolers With Childhood Apraxia of Speech
abstract: Purpose: The aim of this study was to compare retention of real-word targets across practice conditions (contextualized vs. motor-only) within a modified integral stimulation treatment for preschoolers with childhood apraxia of speech (CAS). Method: A single-subject experimental design with alternating treatments was used with matched target sets randomly assigned to contextualized practice, motor-only practice, or no treatment. Three preschoolers with CAS completed 18 therapy sessions, each consisting of two 25-min blocks: one contextualized practice and one motor-only practice. Order of practice was randomized each visit. Changes in percent phonemes correct (PPC) and lexical stress accuracy, derived from blinded transcription, were explored with visual analysis and effect sizes (standardized mean difference, d statistic). title: Speech-Language Pathologists' Confidence and Preparedness Working With Clients With Hearing Loss
abstract: Purpose: The primary purpose of this study was to assess the confidence and preparedness of speech-language pathologists (SLPs) to work with clients with hearing loss across various employment settings. Method: An online Qualtrics survey was used to collect data from respondents currently practicing in the United States and holding the Certificate of Clinical Competence in Speech-Language Pathology. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Multiple linear regressions were employed to assess the relation between confidence level and employment setting. Results: Sixty participants were included in the final analysis. Participants were most confident in checking to make sure devices (i.e., hearing aids, cochlear implants) were on. Working in a hospital setting was associated with higher confidence in working with hearing aids, while working in school settings was associated with lower confidence. title: Paired-Comparison Versus Cross-Sectional Approaches for Assessing Longitudinal Speech Change in Parkinson's Disease Following Deep Brain Stimulation of the Subthalamic Nucleus
abstract: Purpose: Longitudinal changes in perceptual speech outcomes are typically derived from independent judgments at each time point rather than side by side within-speaker comparisons. This study evaluated a paired-comparison method for detecting longitudinal speech change in Parkinson's disease (PD) across three perceptual constructs (intelligibility, listener effort, and severity) relative to a cross-sectional method for detecting speech changes in the same cohort. Method: We collected recordings of the Speech Intelligibility Test at a baseline session and 12-month follow-up from speakers with PD after undergoing subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation implantation surgery and speakers with PD undergoing best medical management. Blinded naive listeners heard the recordings and provided cross-sectional judgments of intelligibility, listener effort, and speech severity. Another set of crowdsourced naive listeners completed a blinded online paired-comparison paradigm and judged changes in the same three constructs between baseline and 12-month sessions. title: Progression of Dysarthria, Drooling, and Swallowing Disorders in Parkinson's Disease: A 1-Year Prospective Cohort Study
abstract: Purpose: Dysarthria, drooling, and swallowing disorders are common motor problems in people with Parkinson's disease (PwP), leading to significant physical, emotional, and functional impairments that compromise quality of life. However, evidence on the progression of these disorders and their relationship with other features of Parkinson's disease (PD) remains scarce. This study aimed to investigate the progression of dysarthria, drooling, and swallowing disorders in PwP and identify predictors of progression. Method: A 1-year prospective cohort study was conducted with 73 PwP. Dysarthria was assessed using the Frenchay Dysarthria Assessment–Second Edition (FDA-2), drooling with Item 2.2 (Saliva and drooling) of the Movement Disorder Society–Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS), and swallowing with the Swallowing Clinical Assessment Score in Parkinson's Disease (SCAS-PD). title: Caregiver-Implemented Early Language Interventions for Latine Children With Language Delays: A Systematic Review
abstract: Purpose: Empowering caregivers with tools to support their children with language delays can potentially increase access to services for families from diverse backgrounds. The purpose of this systematic review was to describe the outcomes and characteristics of caregiver-implemented early language interventions studied or implemented with Spanish-speaking or bilingual Latine children with language delays. We also examined the extent to which these interventions were culturally and linguistically adapted. Method: Six search engines were used to identify articles published between 1990 and 2024. We completed a hand search of reference lists within eligible articles. We completed data extraction with an emphasis on the intervention's characteristics, outcomes for caregivers and children, and cultural and linguistic adaptations. Results: Ten articles were included in this review. Eight caregiver-implemented early language interventions have been studied with Latine children aged 18–47 months from Spanish-speaking families who exhibit language delays. title: Social Isolation in Adults Who Stutter: A Mixed-Methods Investigation of Risk and Correlates
abstract: Purpose: Social isolation is a commonly reported aspect of the stuttering experience. This study qualitatively explored adult stutterers' reports of social isolation while quantitatively examining possible correlates underlying the occurrence of social isolation in this population. Method: A sample of 264 adults who stutter were asked to share their experiences of social isolation and to complete measures of personality, stuttering role identity, social disconnectedness, and perceived isolation via an internet survey. Qualitative data were analyzed via thematic content analysis. Quantitative data were analyzed via linear and ordinal logistic regression to determine the influence of various correlates on social isolation. Results: Qualitative data indicated that the experience of social isolation is common to the experience of living as an adult who stutters. Responses indicated that social isolation in adults who stutter is influenced by personality differences, environmental components, and life experiences. title: Culture-Agnostic and Culture-Specific Analyses of Semantic Fluency in Korean and English Speakers With Alzheimer's Disease
abstract: Purpose: This study investigated cross-linguistic and cultural influences on semantic fluency in monolingual Korean- and English-speaking individuals with Alzheimer's disease (AD) by contrasting culture-agnostic and culture-specific analytic frameworks. We focused on how culturally grounded schemas, such as the East Asian zodiac, shape clustering and switching patterns and on their associations with global cognition. Method: We analyzed semantic fluency in 36 individuals with AD and 30 language-matched older adults using culture-agnostic and culture-specific frameworks. We examined total and first-response proportions of exemplars and compared clustering and switching patterns based on Troyer's taxonomy and a culture-specific scheme that included zodiac animals. All fluency measures were correlated with global cognition. title: Understanding the Concept of Fluency in Stuttering: A Grounded-Theory Study
abstract: Purpose: Fluency is a widely used concept in stuttering research and clinical practice and has traditionally been approached through observable speech characteristics. Although theoretical and clinical perspectives have acknowledged internal aspects of fluency, the perspectives of people who stutter themselves remain largely unexplored. The purpose of this study was to examine how adults who stutter define fluency and experience it in their daily lives. Method: Ten adults who stutter participated in individual interviews guided by an evolved grounded theory approach. Interviews began with the question, “What does fluency mean to you in the context of stuttering?” and follow-up questions were guided by participants' responses. Recruitment continued until saturation was reached. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using grounded-theory analysis. title: The Role of Religion and Spirituality in Clinical Practice: Considerations for Speech-Language Pathologists
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this article is to review the potential role of religion and spirituality in the practice of speech-language pathology and to identify possible clinical resources and directions for future research. Method: We reviewed the literature on health care providers' responses to the religious/spiritual practices of their patients, as well as existing tools for provider self-assessment in this domain. Conclusions: In a diverse and polarized country, it can be difficult for speech-language pathologists to address religious/spiritual practice with the patients and families they serve. These practices, however, may have significant implications for patients' needs and preferences in the domains of speech, language, and swallowing. Clinical tools for addressing these challenges appropriately can be viewed as a component of culturally responsive care.

title: Beyond the Acute Phase: Prevalence and Clinical Characteristics of Unreported Swallowing Impairments in Ambulatory Outpatient Stroke Survivors
abstract: Purpose: Unreported dysphagia, imaging-identified swallowing impairment without symptom reporting, remains poorly characterized beyond the acute phase of stroke. This study aimed to (a) quantify the point prevalence of unreported dysphagia in ambulatory stroke survivors, (b) examine demographic and clinical factors associated with the presentation of this phenomenon, and (c) evaluate concordance between patient-reported symptoms and imaging-derived impairments. Method: This retrospective secondary analysis included 45 ambulatory adults ≥ 3 months post–ischemic stroke who underwent videofluoroscopic swallow study and completed the Eating Assessment Tool-10 (EAT-10). Swallowing impairment was defined using the Dynamic Imaging Grade of Swallowing Toxicity (DIGEST Grade ≥ 1), and physiology was characterized using the Modified Barium Swallow Impairment Profile (MBSImP). Participants were classified as having no dysphagia (DIGEST = 0), overt dysphagia (DIGEST ≥ 1 and EAT-10 > 3), or unreported dysphagia (DIGEST ≥ 1 and EAT-10 ≤ 3). title: Test–Retest Reliability of Core Lexicon Analysis
abstract: Purpose: We examined the test–retest reliability of core lexicon analysis for healthy control participants (HCPs) and individuals with aphasia (IWAs) to facilitate research and clinical implementation of discourse analysis. Method: Transcripts from 50 HCPs and 61 IWAs (from the AphasiaBank database) were used. All participants completed two testing sessions approximately 1 week apart. The AphasiaBank discourse protocol was administered, including a picture scene, two picture sequences, a story retell, and a procedural task. Computerized Language Analysis software was used to score each task for production of previously established core lexicon items. Test–retest reliability was assessed under a generalization theory framework to examine measurement stability, identify the magnitude of differences in core lexicon scores across time for both groups, and examine the contexts for which reliability is sufficient. title: Two Measures, Same Outcome: Comparable Associations Between Exposure Measurements and Language Performance in Bilinguals With and Without Developmental Language Disorder
abstract: Purpose: Language exposure is associated with language performance in bilinguals. Two common ways of measuring language exposure are total hours of exposure and percentage of exposure. This study compared differences in these two methods and examined their associations with bilingual language performance. Differences between typically developing (TD) children and those with developmental language disorder (DLD) were also analyzed across exposure measures and language performance. Method: Participants were 1,397 Spanish–English bilingual preschool children (73 identified with DLD). Caregivers reported hour-by-hour language input and output for a typical weekday and a typical weekend. Children's bilingual language performance was measured using a standardized language screener. Correlation and effect size analyses were calculated. Results: Percentage and total hours of exposure were strongly and significantly correlated for both Spanish and English. Both measures showed moderate, significant correlations with bilingual language performance, with minimal differences in effect sizes. title: Development of a Multimodal Assessment of Mastication Protocol
abstract: Purpose: Within the field of speech-language pathology, the only validated noninstrumental assessment of mastication is the Test of Mastication and Swallowing Solids. This assessment protocol offers limited applicability and ecological validity, as it does not reflect typical meals, which involve greater volume and varied textures. Recognizing the need for a more comprehensive evaluation of mastication, this study aims to develop and evaluate a novel assessment protocol of the oral preparatory phase in healthy participants with typical chewing/swallowing. This protocol includes literature-based measures of masticatory parameters, a color-changing gum, and motion analysis. Method: Using a within-subject design, 50 participants chewed a color-changing gum that was analyzed using Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage L*a*b* (CIELAB) values. Participants chewed a baby carrot, a shortbread cookie, and a Hi-Chew candy. The number of chews was manually counted and further measured using two-dimensional motion analysis. Participants completed a social validity questionnaire evaluating the assessment protocol. CIELAB values were correlated with masticatory parameters using Pearson's r .

title: A Function-Led Tailored Speech-Language Intervention in Primary Progressive Aphasia: A Retrospective Observational Pre–Post Study From Routine Clinical Practice
abstract: Purpose: Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is a neurodegenerative disease that affects language abilities. Since no curative or pharmacological treatments are currently available, speech-language therapy represents one of the few clinical intervention options. Furthermore, evidence from routine clinical practice is needed to better characterize language changes associated with tailored, person-centered speech-language therapy approaches in PPA. The aim of this retrospective observational pre–post study was to explore baseline-to-follow-up changes associated with a function-led tailored speech-language intervention delivered in routine clinical practice. Method: A retrospective pre–post clinical study was conducted on data collected from individuals with a diagnosis of PPA who received weekly 45-min function-led, tailored speech-language therapy in routine clinical practice over 6–9 months. title: Predicting Developmental Language Disorder in Bilinguals From Multiple Sources of Evidence: A Decision Tree Approach
abstract: Purpose: Speech-language pathologists consider multiple pieces of assessment data when making diagnostic decisions for bilingual children. The current study explored the converging evidence framework by applying a decision tree model, a user-friendly prediction tool, to identify bilingual children with developmental language disorder (DLD) using multiple assessment data. Method: One hundred eighty-six Spanish–English bilingual children in kindergarten completed a bilingual language assessment battery, consisting of parents' and teachers' questionnaires, standardized language assessment, narrative sample analysis, and dynamic assessment. Decision tree models were constructed to identify DLD. Results: The decision tree models using (a) bilingual assessment data and (b) bilingual assessment data with parents' and teachers' data as fixed root achieved acceptable sensitivity and specificity. title: Stuttering Treatment Priorities and Clinical Challenges Across the Lifespan in Iran: A Mixed-Methods Study of Speech-Language Pathologists
abstract: Purpose: This study provided an initial exploration of Iranian speech-language pathologists' (SLPs') treatment priorities, reported intervention approaches, and perceived clinical challenges for stuttering across the lifespan. Method: Seventy-four Iranian SLPs completed a Farsi online survey ranking three treatment aspects aligned with the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health—overt stuttering behaviors, reactions to stuttering, and communication participation—across preschool, school-age/adolescent, and adult clients. They also rated intervention use frequency and described clinical challenges. Quantitative data were analyzed using nonparametric tests, qualitative responses were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, and exploratory mixed-methods integration linked clinician priority profiles to qualitative themes. Results: Across all three age groups, clinicians ranked overt behaviors highest, reactions intermediate, and communication participation lowest. title: Clinical Interpretation and Structured Reporting of Velopharyngeal Magnetic Resonance Imaging: A Framework for Multidisciplinary Decision Making
abstract: Purpose: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables direct visualization of the velopharyngeal (VP) mechanism, including the soft palate, pharyngeal walls, adenoid tissue, and levator veli palatini (LVP) musculature. As VP MRI becomes more integrated into multidisciplinary craniofacial care, speech-language pathologists (SLPs) are increasingly involved in image interpretation. However, structured guidance for translating MRI findings into clinically relevant multidisciplinary decision making remains limited. This study presents a clinically oriented framework for interpretation of VP MRI and introduces a structured reporting approach to support consistent documentation and interdisciplinary communication. Method: A literature-informed, consensus-based framework for interpreting VP MRI was developed. Scoping review first identified MRI-derived anatomic variables relevant to VP function. title: A Study of Variability in Brief Assessment of Transactional Success in Aphasia Story Retelling Performance Using Generalizability Theory
abstract: Purpose: This study used generalizability theory (G-theory) to assess the reliability of the Brief Assessment of Transactional Success in aphasia (BATS) and whether reliability can be maintained with more efficient study designs. Method: G-theory was applied to a data set from BATS test development, where story retells were scored using main concept analysis. Linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate the proportion of variability in scores attributable to storyteller (a person with aphasia [PWA] or familiar/unfamiliar conversation partner [CP]), rater (human or automated), and stimuli. Decision studies (D-studies) were conducted to determine the number of stimuli needed for acceptable reliability. Score distributions and correlations were examined to identify stimuli that disproportionately contributed to measurement error. Results: Differences in performance between PWA contributed most to variability in scores, whereas rater contributed minimally. title: The Effects of Multimodal Communication Treatment With Discourse and Group Activities via Telepractice on People With Severe Nonfluent Aphasia: A Case Study
abstract: Purpose: Nonfluent aphasia can be characterized by prominent difficulty with speech production. Compensatory and functional aphasia treatments, including multimodal communication treatment (MCT), have been highlighted for their support of life participation because they aim to circumvent spoken language difficulties through use of other modalities. The current study explored an expanded version of MCT, by including a discourse task and group activities on telepractice (MCT with discourse and group activities via telepractice [teleMCT+DG]) to mirror daily communication and improve communication success for people with severe nonfluent aphasia. Method: Two participants with severe aphasia participated in teleMCT+DG for 10 weeks (two individual and one group treatment sessions per week) to practice five communication modalities (speaking, writing, drawing, gesturing, and using a communication book) during a story generation task. Participants' success of modality production for target items during the story generation task was analyzed. abstract: Purpose: In response to the need for more appropriate anomia treatment materials for bilingual persons with aphasia (BPWAs), we have created linguistically and culturally appropriate versions of AbSANT (Abstract Semantic Associative Network Training) for several languages that we call BAbSANT (Bilingual Abstract Semantic Associative Network Training). BAbSANT has now been conducted with 15 BPWAs in six different language combinations. The purposes of this study were to determine whether BAbSANT produces (a) similar within-language treatment effects as AbSANT and (b) cross-language treatment effects, and to determine whether language dominance affects (a) within- and (b) cross-language generalization. Method: We employed interrupted time series models to analyze all available (published and unpublished) BAbSANT data. abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between latent naming and narrative discourse ability in people with aphasia, extending prior research with a revised discourse measurement model focused on narrative production. Method: Data from 223 participants from AphasiaBank were analyzed (final n = 220). Latent naming ability was indicated by the Boston Naming Test–Short Form, Verb Naming Test, and Western Aphasia Battery–Revised Naming Subtest (WABN). Latent narrative discourse ability, in the context of AphasiaBank's Cinderella storytelling task, was indicated by main concept analysis (MCA) subscores Accurate and Complete (AC), and Attempts (ATT), Sequencing (SEQ), Story Grammar Episodic Complexity (SGEC), and Core Lexicon (CoreLex). title: Reading After Traumatic Brain Injury: Shifts in Engagement, Purpose, and Format Across Everyday Material Types
abstract: Purpose: Reading is central to adult participation in everyday life, yet little is known about how everyday reading habits change following traumatic brain injury (TBI). Prior research has focused primarily on reading speed and comprehension, with less attention to real-world reading behavior. The purpose of this study was to describe and compare everyday reading habits in adults with mild TBI, moderate–severe TBI, and no history of TBI. Method: Survey data from a sequential mixed-methods study of reading after TBI were analyzed for 170 adults with mild TBI, 55 with moderate–severe TBI, and 370 uninjured controls (UC) with no TBI. Everyday reading behavior was assessed using the Reading Habits Inventory, capturing frequency of reading engagement, estimated daily reading time, reading purpose across material types, and format preference (screen vs. physical). title: Navigating Texting With Aphasia: Insights From People With Aphasia and Their Partners
abstract: Purpose: Text messaging is a widely used mode of communication. Like people without aphasia, people with aphasia use texting to communicate with those in their social networks. As the study of texting in aphasia is relatively new, little is known about the impact of aphasia on texting experiences. This study aims to uncover how people with aphasia and their partners navigate text messaging and how texting patterns change throughout recovery. Method: Participants included 15 people with aphasia and a self-selected texting partner. Naturalistic texting data and semistructured interviews were collected and analyzed qualitatively through reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Analyses revealed that people with aphasia and their partners were operating in a dynamic, interactional texting environment that was negotiated over time. title: Partner-Specific Audience Design in Parkinson's Disease: Insights From In-Person and Virtual Modalities
abstract: Purpose: Successful conversation depends on audience design—tailoring utterances to a partner's knowledge. Parkinson's disease (PD) is linked to speech motor and pragmatic impairments, yet it remains unclear whether speakers with PD retain partner-specific audience design. We tested two competing predictions. If previously reported pragmatic deficits generalize, speakers with PD should show attenuated partner sensitivity. If adaptive mechanisms remain intact, audience design should be preserved, particularly in goal-directed interactions. Method: Two referential communication experiments included two phases: sorting (establishing shared labels) and test (assessing partner-specific adaptation) in a single session. title: Inner Speech Can Predict Naming Treatment Outcomes in Aphasia: A Pilot, Single-Subject Design Study
abstract: Purpose: This single-subject design study examined whether self-reported inner speech (IS)—the subjective experience of retrieving a word internally—can predict item-level outcomes in a cueing-based naming treatment for individuals with poststroke aphasia. Method: Five adults with chronic, poststroke aphasia completed an IS self-report task and naming task to identify appropriate treatment stimuli in two categories: successful IS (sIS) and unsuccessful IS (uIS). Participants then completed 2 weeks of hierarchical, cueing-based naming treatment targeting both sIS and uIS items. Treatment effects were analyzed using Tau U and mixed-effects models, with additional insights from visual analysis of individual performance. Results: In four of five participants, naming accuracy improved significantly for sIS items but not for uIS items. The participant who did not show treatment-based learning had the most severe aphasia and apraxia of speech among the group. title: Multimodal Communication in Progressive Aphasia: A Mixed-Methods Experience Sampling Study
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of the experience sampling method (ESM) in characterizing the communication behaviors of individuals with primary progressive aphasia (PPA) and to characterize the use of different communication modalities by five participants with PPA and their care partners. Method: Five dyads (participant with PPA and care partner) completed semistructured interviews followed by a 1-week data collection period. Surveys were delivered twice daily to participants via texted links. Participants reported on their use of communication modalities (speech, gesture, writing, etc.). Feasibility was measured by retention and adherence to the response schedule; acceptability was evaluated using the System Usability Scale and a measure of care partner assistance. Patterns of modality usage across participants were analyzed visually, and interview data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to contextualize ESM findings. title: Self-Reported Inner Speech Reflects Improvement From Language Therapy
abstract: Purpose: This study examined the role of inner speech—defined here as the subjective experience of covert lexical access—in naming recovery following semantic feature analysis (SFA) treatment in individuals with aphasia. Specifically, it tested whether baseline inner speech predicted treatment outcome and whether momentary changes in inner speech across the study were associated with naming success. Method: Eighteen individuals with poststroke aphasia completed three pretreatment naming probes, nine SFA treatment sessions targeting 30 individualized items (Treated30), and three posttreatment probes. On each naming trial, participants indicated whether they experienced inner speech prior to responding. The primary hypothesis—that pretreatment inner speech predicts posttreatment naming accuracy for treated items—was tested using logistic mixed-effects models with participant as a random effect. title: Personalization of Words in Anomia Treatment for People With Aphasia: A Scoping Review
abstract: Purpose: This scoping review examined how “personalization” of treatment targets, specifically words, has been defined and implemented in anomia interventions for people with aphasia following stroke or primary progressive aphasia. The review identified (a) how studies define personalized words, (b) the methods used to select them, and (c) the linguistic characteristics of personalized targets. Method: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews, systematic searches were conducted in MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and CINAHL on July 8, 2024, with no date limits. Data extraction captured how personalization was defined or described, word selection methods, involvement of participants and partners, and linguistic characteristics. title: Comparing the Community-Identified and Federally Funded Rehabilitation Priorities for Stroke Survivors With Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: Person-centered rehabilitation for stroke survivors with aphasia (SSwAs) targets meaningful recovery goals using interventions supported by strong scientific evidence. To maximize clinical impact, aphasia research should provide evidence that directly supports person-centered recovery goals. The purpose of this project was to characterize and compare the rehabilitation priorities of SSwAs living in the United States to the research priorities of federally funded aphasia clinical trials. Method: Community-identified priorities were characterized by a narrative literature review. title: Addressing Diagnostic Challenges in Acquired Apraxia of Speech: A Preliminary Study to Inform Curriculum Development
abstract: Purpose: Acquired apraxia of speech (AOS) frequently co-occurs with aphasia and/or dysarthria, complicating accurate and reliable diagnosis for speech-language pathologists (SLPs). To address this challenge, this preliminary study explored the diagnostic processes and decision making of SLPs during recorded evaluations of persons with aphasia with potential co-occurring AOS and/or dysarthria, with the ultimate goal of informing the development of a training curriculum to improve diagnostic accuracy. Method: Eight licensed SLPs participated and viewed recorded videos of eight individuals with aphasia and potential motor speech impairments. Stimuli included the spoken language subtests of Western Aphasia Battery–Revised and a standard motor speech exam. After viewing, SLPs were asked to complete the Apraxia of Speech Rating Scale (ASRS) and two questionnaires focusing on the diagnostic processes. title: Toward a Diagnostic Template for Acquired Apraxia of Speech: Insights From an Academy of Neurologic Communication Disorders Review
abstract: Purpose: Significant variation is observed in diagnostic assessments for individuals with acquired apraxia of speech (AOS). The lack of consistency across research related to AOS impacts the comparison of intervention outcomes. This extends to diagnostic criteria, assessment, and the inclusion of patient demographics. This viewpoint examines outcomes related to the consistency in diagnostic tool use and collection of demographic information and introduces a template to support researchers and clinicians conducting diagnostic evaluations. Materials include guidelines for a thorough case history, current diagnostic characteristics, and diagnostic assessment tools available for describing AOS. title: “It's Hard Hard to Hard to Make It That Way. But You Gotta Make It All Different Levels”: Making Aphasia Groups Work From the Perspective of People With Severe Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: Facilitators require further guidance on best practices to support people with severe aphasia (PWSA) who attend their aphasia groups. In this study, we position PWSA as experts who can inform future research and practice patterns. The aim of this study was to explore the ideas PWSA have regarding how aphasia groups should function with a specific focus on aspects that relate to meeting their needs, given the severity of their aphasia. Method: We analyzed data from interviews with five PWSA that were completed as part of a larger project. For this study, we used qualitative content analysis with a descriptive explorative approach, grounded in a constructivist paradigm. title: The Cognitive Substrates of Action Fluency: A Multivariate Analysis in Parkinson's Disease
abstract: Purpose: Action fluency (AF), the rapid generation of verbs, has been proposed as a sensitive marker of cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, it is unclear whether AF reflects domain-general executive–generative abilities or a disease-specific motor semantic deficit. This study examined the cognitive predictors of AF in individuals with PD without dementia (PD-ND). Method: Thirty-one older adults (14 PD-ND, 17 healthy controls) matched on age, sex, and education completed AF, letter fluency, semantic fluency, design fluency, processing speed, and global cognition tasks. AF responses were scored for unique verbs. title: A Novel Treatment of Error Awareness for Acquired Apraxia of Speech and Aphasia: Effects of a Single-Case Experimental Design Investigation
abstract: Purpose: Error awareness (EA) is the ability to identify errors in one's speech productions. Persons with aphasia and apraxia of speech (A-AOS) have been found to vary widely in their EA abilities. EA, as measured by the accuracy of self-judgments of word production accuracy, has been found to be moderately associated with response to AOS treatment. EA training has rarely been included in AOS treatments, and the impact of EA as a treatment ingredient has not been studied. This study was designed to examine the effects of a novel treatment for impaired EA in individuals with A-AOS—the Treatment of Error Awareness (TEA). Method: Two participants with chronic A-AOS received TEA applied to multisyllabic words in the context of a multiple-baseline design. TEA therapeutic ingredients included repetition of modeled words, judgment of self-productions, and a response-contingent hierarchy focused on facilitating awareness of auditory and somatosensory feedback. title: Cross-Linguistic Insights From the Boston Naming Test: Structural Comparability and Performance Comparisons of English and Korean Speakers With Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: This study examined the structural comparability of the English and Korean versions of the Boston Naming Test (E-BNT and K-BNT) and evaluated whether structural similarity translates into comparable performance patterns in individuals with aphasia. Method: In Study 1, we analyzed two psycholinguistic features—lexical frequency and syllable length—across the E-BNT and K-BNT. title: Implementation Science: Buzzword or Game Changer? Ten Years Later
abstract: Purpose: Implementation science was introduced to increase the uptake of evidence-based practices in acquired neurogenic communication disorders with the goal of transforming care for people with aphasia, dementia, and related conditions. Over time, its growing body of terminology and frameworks risks creating a parallel research-to-practice gap, distancing the field from the very improvements it was meant to achieve. This tutorial draws on 10 years of applied research and clinical work to clarify how implementation science can improve the realities of care. Method: This tutorial distills five practice- and research-informed lessons drawn from a decade of applied research and clinical work including: (a) get closer to how care actually happens in everyday practice, (b) design approaches that reach those most often left out of studies, (c) view fidelity and adaptation as dual processes, (d) account for organizational and systemic realities, and (e) accelerate learning through rapid small-scale cycles of change. title: Preliminary Reliability and Validity of Asynchronous Speech Screening to Support Clinical Triage for Children With Cleft Palate and Velopharyngeal Dysfunction
abstract: Purpose: Children with cleft and craniofacial conditions require ongoing monitoring and evaluation to manage persistent speech and resonance disorders. Regular assessment allows clinicians to detect emerging problems, evaluate intervention efficacy, and adjust treatment plans accordingly. However, socioeconomic and logistical barriers place many children at risk for sporadic or absent follow-up, leading to undiagnosed or underaddressed velopharyngeal dysfunction. title: “A Better Way of Just Being Free”: Exploring How Stroke Survivors With Aphasia Experienced an Intervention Combining Communication Strategy Training With Acceptance and Commitment Therapy
abstract: Purpose: Depression, anxiety, and social isolation are prevalent among stroke survivors with aphasia (SSwA). However, evidence-based mental health interventions for SSwA are limited. The Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) for Aphasia Phase I clinical trial (NCT04984239) sought to bridge this gap by adapting and piloting an intervention combining ACT with communication strategy training to improve mental health and functional communication in SSwA. Here, we present the qualitative findings of this study to characterize experiential outcomes and inform intervention refinement. title: “Curious but Overwhelmed”: Care Partner Perspectives on Education, Resources, and Coping After Aphasia Diagnosis
abstract: Purpose: Care partners of people with aphasia (PWA) are faced with unique challenges, as their loved one's loss of communication may create specific barriers to expression, mutual understanding, and interaction. Previous research has investigated the challenges faced by care partners of PWA. However, there is limited research that investigates the perceived aphasia education needs of these care partners. The purpose of the present study is to investigate the perspectives of care partners on education, challenges, benefits, and supports they experience when caring for a loved one with aphasia. This work may provide insight into the complexities of the experience of living as a care partner of someone with aphasia. abstract: Purpose: Changes in graduate-level clinical reasoning for clinical swallow evaluation were examined and compared between video simulation and standardized patient simulation training. title: From Policy to Practice: A Speech-Language Pathologist's Guide to Advancing Communication Access Through Accommodations
abstract: Purpose: In health care settings, people with communication disabilities (CDs) are more likely to experience ineffective communication and worse outcomes. A substantial contributor is the absence of routine accommodations: modifications to practices and procedures, and aids and services provided by the health care team to enable equitable access to care. Federal law, including the Americans with Disabilities Act, requires health care teams to provide accommodations. abstract: Background: Research has demonstrated that many speech-language pathologists (SLPs) have reported having reduced knowledge and competence in the assessment and intervention of children and adults who stutter and clutter. abstract: Purpose: Anterior open bite (AOB) is a multifactorial malocclusion frequently associated with nonnutritive sucking habits (NNSHs) and orofacial dysfunctions. title: Best Practice International Guidelines on Online Communities of Aphasia Groups
abstract: Purpose: We aim to establish best practice guidelines for the design, facilitation, and sustainability of online support groups for people with aphasia (PWA). It explores the benefits, challenges, and psychological considerations of virtual aphasia interventions. Method: The recommendations presented were developed through a collaborative consensus process by our writing team, which was informed by a comprehensive review of current literature, insights from international experts, and practical experiences across various settings. title: Word Retrieval in the Wild: The Feasibility of an Audio-Based Ecological Momentary Naming Protocol Completed by Adults With and Without Poststroke Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) involves collecting data regarding behaviors or states of interest repeatedly in individuals' natural environments, typically from a smart device. The feasibility of EMA protocols with people with aphasia (PWA) remains relatively unexplored, particularly for objective assessments of language ability. We assessed the feasibility of a novel, smartwatch-delivered, audio-based ecological momentary naming protocol. abstract: Purpose: The present study aimed at evaluating the impact of a voice amplification system plus vocal hygiene on aerodynamic, acoustic, and self-reported outcomes in elementary school teachers with and without voice problems. abstract: Purpose: Following conversations at the 2026 International Cognitive-Communication Disorders Conference, this viewpoint advocates for the principled development of technology-based memory rehabilitation after traumatic brain injury (TBI) and presents an illustrative example for maximizing resources in the development of new interventions. Method: This viewpoint discusses how technology may address key unmet needs in TBI memory rehabilitation, the design fundamentals for this line of work, and an illustrative example of relevant guiding principles for technology-delivered intervention development. abstract: Purpose: The fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1 ( FMR1 ) premutation (FXpm) is a prevalent genetic variant that confers risk for neurodegenerative motor impairments associated with fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS). abstract: Purpose: The aim of this study was to better understand the functional implications of late talking by documenting the lived experiences of parenting a late-talking toddler.
